claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the balance between nucleation speed and atomic diffusion.
Rapid quenching during reduction kinetically traps atoms in a disordered high-entropy state.
Kinetic trapping occurs before significant surface diffusion can take place.
Rapid quenching suppresses elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching suppresses phase separation.
Slower processing permits greater atomic rearrangement.
Surface-energy differences drive atomic rearrangement toward heterogeneous structures under slower processing.
The competition between nucleation and diffusion mediates final alloy homogeneity.
A fast reduction rate limits the time available for surface or interfacial atomic diffusion.
Kinetic trapping preserves a uniform high-entropy alloy structure.
Fast processing preserves significant surface-atom exposure.
Significant surface-atom exposure is beneficial for catalysis.
Nanoparticles produced under fast-quenching conditions will have a more homogeneous elemental distribution than those produced under slower conditions.
Nanoparticles produced under fast-quenching conditions will have better-controlled morphology than those produced under slower conditions.
Slower processing will produce discernible phase separation and segregated elemental domains.
Slower processing will increase morphological irregularity.
Prior comparative evidence indicates that moderate-rate baseline synthesis commonly produces elemental segregation and uncontrolled morphology.
Elemental segregation and uncontrolled morphology reduce catalytic surface availability.
The proposed mechanism applies when disparities in reduction kinetics and surface energies among the noble-metal precursors are moderate.
The proposed mechanism may fail when reduction-potential disparities are extreme or when post-synthesis thermal processing substantially changes diffusion.
